notes.claim: Voltage drop is (mV/A/m) × Ib × length / 1000, where mV/A/m is millivolts dropped per ampere of design current per metre, taken from the Appendix 4 cable tables.
The limits are 3% of the supply voltage for lighting and 5% for other circuits (6.9 V and 11.5 V on 230 V); the slides say to use a given supply voltage, so 5% of 395 V is 19.75 V.
The drop counts from the origin to the most distant point, so the submain's drop is added to the final circuit's; the formula sheet and project guide both say so.

When a three-phase submain feeds a single-phase final circuit, the formula sheet divides the submain's three-phase voltage drop by root 3 before adding it, and the project guide warns to calculate this correctly.
If the first cable fails, the slides increase the conductor CSA and repeat ("chasing the volt drop"); 1.5 mm² over 85 m fails, and 6.0 mm² gives 8.09 V.

The tabulated mV/A/m values are for the maximum conductor operating temperature, reached only at full load; at lower loads the cable is cooler and its resistance lower, which the factor Ct corrects (the Ct formula itself was not captured).
For cables above 16 mm² the tables give R, X and Z; the slides use Z where no power factor is known and R and X where one is.
